Question: A particular \(12\)-hour digital clock displays the hour and minute of a day. Unfortunately, whenever it is supposed to display a \(1,\) it mistakenly displays a \(9.\) For example, when it is \(1{:}16\) pm the clock incorrectly shows \(9{:}96\) pm. What fraction of the day will the clock show the correct time?
Solution:
The clock is correct exactly when the intended display contains no digit \(1\). Its 12-hour pattern repeats twice each day, so we can count within one cycle of \(12\cdot60=720\) equal one-minute intervals.

The hour labels containing no \(1\) are \(2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\), giving \(8\) choices. The excluded hours are \(1,10,11,12\).

Minutes run from \(00\) to \(59\). Their tens digit can be \(0,2,3,4,5\), giving \(5\) choices, and their units digit can be any digit except \(1\), giving \(9\) choices. Every such pair is a valid minute label, so there are \(5\cdot9=45\) permissible minutes in each permissible hour.

Each hour-and-minute choice identifies exactly one interval, and every correct display is included. Thus the fraction of the cycle, and of the day, with a correct display is
\[
\frac{8\cdot45}{12\cdot60}=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
choice A.
